title: Adhesive Interfacial Crack in Bonded Joints
introduction: Adhesive interfacial cracking is the structural failure of the adhesive-adherend bond in bonded joints used to attach flexible photovoltaic module components. When mechanical loading is applied to joints that contain voids or bonding-area defects, stress concentrates at the defect boundaries, causing crack initiation along the adhesive-adherend interface. The resulting interfacial crack propagates along the bond line, producing a mixed failure mode that combines adhesive debonding along the interface and cohesive fracture within the adhesive layer. This failure directly reduces the mechanical load-bearing capacity of the joint, measured as tensile-shear strength.
reasoning: The 337-Elsevier adhesive bonded joint study directly observes interfacial crack initiation around defects and quantifies the resulting reduction in tensile-shear strength as the structural performance consequence of this failure mode.

key_findings.claim: Cracks initiate along the adhesive-adherend interface around bonding defects under mechanical load
key_findings.detail: When the adhesive joint contains bonding-area defects, cracks are prone to initiate along the interface between the adhesive and the upper adherend in the region surrounding the defect. [^elsevier337a] A mixed failure mode combining adhesive failure and cohesive failure within the adhesive layer is the observed fracture pattern around these defect-initiated cracks. [^elsevier337b]

key_findings.claim: Larger bonding defects produce larger adhesive-fractured regions and lower tensile-shear strength
key_findings.detail: As the diameter of the bonding defect increases, the tensile-shear strength of the joint decreases further. [^elsevier337c] A centrally located defect brings a larger adhesive-fractured region, making the joint's tensile-shear strength lower, while adhesive failure more readily occurs around the defects. [^elsevier337d]
